Explain it to me properly. In the States you apply to twelve places and they look at everything — grades, essays, sport. How does it work here?
Almost nothing like that. Here you are selected by one exam. Two days, and that is the whole thing.
One exam. So nothing else is looked at at all?
At the big public universities, essentially no. The criteria are published in advance and they do not change. Nothing else is considered.
That is either much fairer than ours or much worse, and I honestly cannot decide which.
Both, I think. It is widely believed to be fair, because everybody undergoes exactly the same two days. But everything before those two days is not equal at all.
And what happens after? How do you even find out?

Good morning, and welcome. I am going to describe what happens to your application after you send it, because it is the part nobody explains and the part everybody worries about. Your file is received and checked first. Anything missing is requested once, by email, and only once. Complete files are then passed to two readers, who work separately and who do not know each other's scores. Where the two scores are close, the decision is made there. Where they are far apart, the file is sent to a third reader, and the first two scores are not shown to that person. Decisions are published on a single day, at the same hour, for everybody. Nothing is decided before that day, and nothing is decided by one person alone.

Every writing guide tells you to avoid the passive, and the advice is repeated so often that almost nobody asks where it came from. Here is the honest version. The passive is not weak. It is a tool with one job: it puts the important thing at the front. If the important thing is the person, use the active. If the important thing is what happened, the passive is not only allowed, it is the correct choice. Where the advice is right is where the passive is used to hide somebody. Mistakes were made. The account was closed. Notice that in both of those there is a person missing who ought to be there. So the rule is not avoid the passive. The rule is: know who you left out, and be able to say why.

Two countries, the same problem: far more applicants than places, and no way to make everybody happy. In the first, candidates are ranked by a single examination taken on the same two days by everyone, and nothing else is considered at all. In the second, applications are read one by one, and grades, essays, references and activities are all weighed together by a committee. Each system is defended fiercely by the country that uses it, and each is described as obviously fairer than the other. What the research suggests is less comfortable than either side would like. Both systems predict the first year well and the fifth year badly, and in both of them the strongest single predictor of the result is something that was decided long before the application: where the candidate went to school.
